overview: The dimensions of data quality are the measurable axes along which the 'goodness' of a dataset is judged: completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity, and uniqueness.

Each dimension answers a different question about the data (Is anything missing? Is it correct? Do systems agree? Is it fresh? Does it conform to rules? Are there duplicates?) and each maps to a concrete, automatable check inside a data pipeline.

Frameworks like Great Expectations, dbt tests, Soda, Amazon Deequ, and observability platforms like Monte Carlo let engineers express these dimension checks as code and enforce them before bad data reaches dashboards and models.
learningObjectives: Define all six core data quality dimensions and explain, in plain terms, what each one measures.
Translate every dimension into a concrete metric and an automated check that can run in a real pipeline (e.g., completeness -> null rate, uniqueness -> duplicate count).
Explain the classic validity-versus-accuracy distinction and know which dimensions can be checked automatically versus which need a source of truth.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: The dimensions of data quality are a structured set of measurable attributes (completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity, and uniqueness) that together quantify how fit a dataset is for its intended use. Each dimension is expressed as a metric compared against a threshold or baseline, and enforced through validation rules, statistical profiling, and continuous monitoring within data pipelines.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of data quality dimensions as a checklist you run over a table. Completeness asks 'is anything missing?', accuracy asks 'is it actually right?', consistency asks 'do my systems agree?', timeliness asks 'is it fresh enough?', validity asks 'does it follow the rules I defined?', and uniqueness asks 'are there duplicates?'. Each question turns into a simple calculation you can run on the data automatically.
coreConcept.historicalContext: The idea of decomposing data quality into named dimensions was formalized by Richard Wang and Diane Strong in their 1996 MIT paper, which grouped data quality attributes into intrinsic, contextual, representational, and accessibility categories. Over time the industry converged on a practical shortlist (often six dimensions) popularized by bodies like DAMA. The modern era operationalized these dimensions in pipelines with tools such as Great Expectations (2018), dbt tests, Soda, and Amazon Deequ, and the data observability movement (Monte Carlo, ~2019) turned dimensional monitoring into a continuous, automated practice.

whyItMatters.business: Each dimension protects a different business outcome: completeness protects accurate aggregates, uniqueness protects revenue counts from double-counting, timeliness protects decisions from staleness, and accuracy protects trust in the numbers executives act on.
whyItMatters.engineering: Naming dimensions gives engineers a shared vocabulary and a checklist, so instead of vaguely 'checking the data' they systematically map every dimension to a specific test that fails loudly when broken.
whyItMatters.scalability: As sources multiply, you cannot eyeball quality; expressing each dimension as a metric lets you compute it programmatically across thousands of tables and track it over time.
whyItMatters.cost: Knowing which dimension broke tells you exactly what to fix, avoiding expensive downstream reprocessing, model retraining, or corrected executive reports.
whyItMatters.reliability: Dimensions become the SLIs of data reliability (freshness lag, null rate, duplicate count), letting teams set SLAs and prove data-product reliability the way uptime SLOs do for services.

coreComponents.name: Completeness
coreComponents.definition: The extent to which all required values and records are present, with no unexpected missing data.
coreComponents.purpose: To ensure aggregates, joins, and models are not silently skewed by missing values or dropped rows.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Measure null rates per column, verify mandatory fields are populated, and confirm expected record counts arrived.
coreComponents.examples: Percentage of non-null email values; expected 1,000,000 daily events but only 600,000 arrived (40% missing records).

coreComponents.name: Accuracy
coreComponents.definition: The degree to which a value correctly reflects the real-world entity or event it represents.
coreComponents.purpose: To ensure the data is not just well-formed but actually true, so decisions are based on reality.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Compare values against a trusted source of truth, reference data, or reconciliation totals.
coreComponents.examples: A customer's stored address matches the address on their verified ID; a transaction amount matches the payment processor's record.

coreComponents.name: Consistency
coreComponents.definition: The absence of contradictions for the same fact across records, tables, or systems.
coreComponents.purpose: To ensure the same entity is described the same way everywhere, so reconciliation and joins hold together.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Cross-check the same field between systems, enforce referential integrity, and detect contradictory duplicate facts.
coreComponents.examples: A customer's birthdate is identical in the CRM and the billing system; every order's customer_id exists in the customers table.

coreComponents.name: Timeliness
coreComponents.definition: Whether data is available when expected and reflects a sufficiently recent state (freshness and latency).
coreComponents.purpose: To ensure decisions and dashboards are based on current data, not stale snapshots.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Measure freshness lag (now minus latest timestamp), track arrival time against SLAs, and alert on delays.
coreComponents.examples: The orders table is refreshed by 6 AM daily; the latest event_timestamp is never more than 2 hours old during business hours.

coreComponents.name: Validity
coreComponents.definition: Whether data conforms to defined formats, data types, ranges, and business rules.
coreComponents.purpose: To ensure values are well-formed so downstream parsing, logic, and constraints do not break.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Check formats via regex, enforce accepted-value sets and ranges, and validate data types.
coreComponents.examples: Email matches an email regex; status is one of ['placed','shipped','delivered','cancelled']; age is between 0 and 120.

coreComponents.name: Uniqueness
coreComponents.definition: The absence of unwanted duplicate records or key collisions.
coreComponents.purpose: To ensure counts, sums, and joins are not inflated by the same entity appearing more than once.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Compare COUNT versus COUNT(DISTINCT) on keys, detect duplicate business rows, and enforce primary-key uniqueness.
coreComponents.examples: order_id appears exactly once; no two rows share the same (email, signup_date) combination.

internalWorking: Profiling first scans each column to compute the statistics that make dimension checks possible: null counts (completeness), distinct counts (uniqueness), min/max and value distributions (validity), latest timestamps (timeliness), and reference sets used for cross-checks (consistency).

Completeness and uniqueness are computed as counting problems: completeness compares COUNT(column) to COUNT(*) to derive a null rate, while uniqueness compares COUNT(*) to COUNT(DISTINCT key) so any positive difference reveals duplicates.

Validity is evaluated row by row against declarative rules, typically as the fraction of rows whose value matches a regex, falls in an accepted set, or lies within a numeric range, producing a percentage-invalid metric.

Timeliness is computed as a time delta, subtracting the maximum event or load timestamp from the current time to get a freshness lag that is compared against an SLA, while consistency joins the dataset to a reference source and counts contradictions or orphaned keys.

Accuracy, which cannot be self-checked from the data alone, is measured by reconciling against an external source of truth (a golden record, a control total, or a sampled manual audit) and reporting the match rate; every dimension metric is then compared to a threshold and either passes, fails, or trips an anomaly alert.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Source -> Ingest to staging -> Profile columns (null/distinct/min/max/latest ts) -> Run dimension checks (completeness -> null rate | validity -> regex/range | uniqueness -> dup count | timeliness -> freshness lag | consistency -> reference join | accuracy -> reconcile to source of truth) -> Pass: load to trusted layer | Fail: quarantine + alert -> Store metrics over time -> Anomaly detection / SLA tracking -> Dashboards & alerts
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A daily orders batch lands in staging; a profiling step computes per-column null counts, distinct counts, min/max amounts, and the latest order_date.
2. Completeness runs first: null rate on order_id is 0% and on email is 2%, both within threshold, so the batch passes completeness.
3. Uniqueness compares COUNT(*)=120,357 to COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)=120,345, revealing 12 duplicate order_ids that trip the uniqueness check.

4. Validity checks the amount range (>=0) and email regex, timeliness checks that hours_since_latest is under the 6-hour SLA, and consistency confirms every customer_id exists in the customers dimension.

5. The 12 duplicate rows are routed to a quarantine table with the failed-rule annotation, the batch is marked failed for the uniqueness metric, an alert fires to the data owner, and all passing rows continue to the trusted layer while the metric row is written to history for trend analysis.

keyTerminology.meaning: The extent to which all required data (values and records) is present, with no unexpected gaps.
keyTerminology.importance: Missing values skew averages and break joins; measured via null rates per column and expected-vs-actual record counts.

keyTerminology.meaning: The degree to which data correctly reflects the real-world entity or event it represents.
keyTerminology.importance: The hardest dimension to verify because it usually requires an external source of truth; inaccurate data leads directly to wrong decisions.

keyTerminology.meaning: The absence of contradictions for the same fact across records, tables, or systems.
keyTerminology.importance: Inconsistent values (a customer with two different birthdates across systems) undermine reconciliation and trust.

keyTerminology.meaning: Whether data is available when expected and reflects a sufficiently recent state (freshness plus latency).
keyTerminology.importance: Stale data leads to decisions on outdated information; enforced via freshness lag metrics and arrival SLAs.

keyTerminology.meaning: Whether data conforms to defined formats, data types, ranges, and business rules.
keyTerminology.importance: Invalid values (malformed emails, out-of-range ages) break downstream parsing and logic; checkable automatically via regex, ranges, and accepted sets.

keyTerminology.meaning: The absence of unwanted duplicate records or key collisions.
keyTerminology.importance: Duplicates inflate counts and revenue and corrupt joins; detected by comparing COUNT to COUNT(DISTINCT) on the key.

importantConcepts.explanation: What: validity means a value follows a defined rule or format (email matches the email regex, age is 0-120), while accuracy means the value is actually true in the real world. Why: it is the single most tested distinction because the two are easily confused. How: validity is checked automatically against a rule with no external data; accuracy needs a source of truth (a verified record, a control total) to compare against. Pitfall: assuming a passing validity check proves correctness. A perfectly formatted but wrong phone number is valid yet inaccurate.

importantConcepts.concept: Turning a dimension into a metric
importantConcepts.explanation: What: every dimension must become a single number you can threshold (completeness -> null rate, uniqueness -> duplicate count, timeliness -> freshness lag hours). Why: pipelines can only gate on measurable values, not vague notions of quality. How: compute the metric with a set-based SQL aggregate or a framework expectation, then compare it to a threshold or historical baseline. Pitfall: defining a dimension without a concrete metric, which makes it impossible to automate or alert on.

What: five dimensions (completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness) can be checked from the data plus reference tables, but accuracy generally cannot. Why: knowing this tells you where automation ends and human/reconciliation processes begin. How: automate the five with dbt/Great Expectations/Soda, and handle accuracy through reconciliation to an external system or sampled audits. Pitfall: promising 'we check accuracy automatically' when the pipeline only checks validity.

variationsAndTypes: **Completeness variants:** value-level completeness (null rate on a column) versus record-level completeness (expected vs actual row counts).
**Validity variants:** type validity, format validity (regex), range validity (min/max), and accepted-value-set validity (enums).
**Uniqueness variants:** primary-key uniqueness (one column) versus composite/business-key uniqueness (a set of columns) versus fuzzy duplicate detection.
**Consistency variants:** cross-system consistency, referential integrity within a warehouse, and cross-field logical consistency (e.g., ship_date >= order_date).
**Timeliness variants:** freshness (how recent the latest record is) versus punctuality/latency (did the batch arrive by its scheduled SLA time).
advantages: **Shared vocabulary:** Dimensions give engineers, analysts, and stakeholders a common language for what 'good data' means.
**Directly automatable:** Five of the six dimensions map cleanly to set-based checks that run in-pipeline.
**Pinpoints failures:** Knowing which dimension broke (e.g., uniqueness) tells you exactly what to investigate and fix.
**Enables SLAs:** Dimension metrics become measurable SLIs (freshness lag, null rate, duplicate count) you can commit to.
disadvantages: **Accuracy is hard:** Accuracy usually cannot be verified from the data alone and needs an external source of truth.
**Dimensions overlap:** Validity, consistency, and accuracy can blur, causing confusion about which check to apply.
**Metric definitions vary:** Teams define completeness or timeliness differently, so numbers are not comparable without agreed definitions.
**Passing checks is not full correctness:** Green checks only prove the asserted dimensions, not every possible defect.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Apply the full set of dimension checks on high-value, widely consumed, or regulated data products (financial reporting, ML training data, customer-facing metrics) and at ingestion boundaries where untrusted data enters.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid heavyweight per-dimension checks on transient intermediate tables or exploratory one-off analyses; instead sample or run a lightweight subset (completeness and freshness) where full validation is not worth the cost.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: The dimensions are like a home inspection checklist before you buy a house. Completeness asks whether every room and fixture is actually there; validity asks whether the wiring meets code; accuracy asks whether the listed square footage is truly correct (you need to measure it against a trusted survey); consistency asks whether the blueprints match the actual building; timeliness asks whether the inspection reflects the house's current condition; and uniqueness asks whether you are not accidentally being shown two listings for the same house. Each is a separate question with its own way of checking.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Validity and accuracy are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Validity means the value follows a rule (a well-formed email), while accuracy means it is actually correct (the person's real email). A value can pass validity and still be inaccurate; accuracy needs a source of truth to confirm.

commonMisconceptions.myth: All six dimensions can be checked automatically inside the pipeline.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, and uniqueness can be computed from the data and reference tables, but accuracy generally requires reconciliation against an external source of truth or sampled human audits.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Compute all dimension metrics in a single set-based SQL pass pushed down to the warehouse, filter by partition for incremental loads, and use approximate distinct counts (HyperLogLog) for uniqueness on huge tables.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Fix explicit, agreed definitions for each dimension metric, version them with pipeline code, and make checks deterministic so a completeness or uniqueness number means the same thing every run.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Quarantine rows that fail row-level dimensions (validity, uniqueness) rather than dropping them, so a single bad column does not lose the whole batch and failures can be reprocessed.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Store each dimension's metric (null rate, duplicate count, freshness lag) over time and baseline it, so you catch gradual degradation, not just hard threshold breaches.
productionConsiderations.security: Profiling and quarantine outputs can expose PII (invalid emails, mismatched records); mask sensitive failing values and restrict access to quality artifacts.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Run cheap dimensions (completeness, freshness) frequently and expensive ones (accuracy reconciliation, distribution/consistency joins) on a cadence, and sample where exact numbers are unnecessary.
productionConsiderations.performance: Prefer set-based aggregate SQL over row-by-row Python for completeness/uniqueness/validity, and combine multiple dimension metrics into one scan to avoid repeated full-table reads.

codeExamples.title: Measuring Every Dimension with pandas (Python)
codeExamples.overview: Compute a concrete metric for each of the six dimensions on an orders dataframe, including completeness %, duplicate count, validity via regex, and freshness lag.
codeExamples.code:
import re
import pandas as pd
from datetime import datetime, timezone

df = pd.read_parquet("orders.parquet")
rows = len(df)

# Completeness: percentage of non-null required values
completeness_pct = df["order_id"].notna().mean() * 100
email_completeness = df["email"].notna().mean() * 100

# Uniqueness: duplicate count on the primary key
duplicate_count = rows - df["order_id"].nunique()

# Validity: fraction of emails matching an email regex
email_re = re.compile(r"^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$")
valid_email_mask = df["email"].fillna("").apply(lambda v: bool(email_re.match(v)))
pct_invalid_email = (1 - valid_email_mask.mean()) * 100

# Validity (range): amounts must be non-negative
pct_negative_amount = (df["amount"] < 0).mean() * 100

# Consistency: order rows whose customer_id is missing from the dimension
customers = pd.read_parquet("customers.parquet")
orphans = (~df["customer_id"].isin(customers["customer_id"])).sum()

# Timeliness: freshness lag in hours from the latest order
latest = pd.to_datetime(df["order_date"]).max()
freshness_lag_hours = (datetime.now(timezone.utc) - latest.tz_localize("UTC")).total_seconds() / 3600

print(f"completeness_order_id_pct={completeness_pct:.2f}")
print(f"email_completeness_pct={email_completeness:.2f}")
print(f"duplicate_order_ids={duplicate_count}")
print(f"pct_invalid_email={pct_invalid_email:.2f}")
print(f"pct_negative_amount={pct_negative_amount:.2f}")
print(f"consistency_orphan_customer_ids={orphans}")
print(f"freshness_lag_hours={freshness_lag_hours:.1f}")
codeExamples.breakdown: Each block maps to one dimension: completeness uses notna().mean() to get the non-null percentage; uniqueness subtracts nunique() from the row count to get duplicates; validity applies an email regex and a non-negative range test to get percentage-invalid metrics; consistency uses isin() against the customers dimension to count orphaned keys; timeliness subtracts the max order_date from now to get a freshness lag in hours. Accuracy is intentionally absent because it needs an external source of truth to reconcile against.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
completeness_order_id_pct=100.00
email_completeness_pct=98.10
duplicate_order_ids=12
pct_invalid_email=0.40
pct_negative_amount=0.00
consistency_orphan_customer_ids=3
freshness_lag_hours=2.1
codeExamples.commonIssues: Timezone-naive timestamps breaking the freshness subtraction; a too-loose email regex passing malformed addresses; pulling a huge table into pandas instead of computing in the warehouse.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: For large tables push these metrics into SQL and only bring back the single metric row; wrap each metric in a threshold comparison so the script exits non-zero on breach; store the metric row in a history table for anomaly detection.

codeExamples.title: Per-Dimension Metric Queries in SQL
codeExamples.overview: A single SQL pass that produces one metric per dimension so a wrapper job can compare each to its threshold and fail or alert.
codeExamples.code:
SELECT
  COUNT(*)                                                       AS row_count,
  -- Completeness: percentage of non-null required column
  100.0 * COUNT(order_id) / COUNT(*)                             AS completeness_order_id_pct,
  100.0 * COUNT(email)    / COUNT(*)                             AS completeness_email_pct,
  -- Uniqueness: duplicate keys
  COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)                            AS duplicate_order_ids,
  -- Validity: bad format / out of range
  100.0 * AVG(CASE WHEN email NOT LIKE '%_@_%._%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pct_invalid_email,
  100.0 * AVG(CASE WHEN amount < 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)            AS pct_negative_amount,
  100.0 * AVG(CASE WHEN status NOT IN ('placed','shipped','delivered','cancelled')
                   THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                           AS pct_invalid_status,
  -- Timeliness: freshness lag
  MAX(order_date)                                               AS latest_order,
  DATEDIFF('hour', MAX(order_date), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)          AS freshness_lag_hours
FROM staging.orders
WHERE order_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 day';

-- Consistency (referential integrity) as a separate anti-join
SELECT COUNT(*) AS orphan_customer_ids
FROM staging.orders o
LEFT JOIN dim.customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL;
codeExamples.breakdown: The first query computes completeness (non-null percentage), uniqueness (COUNT vs COUNT(DISTINCT)), validity (conditional averages for bad email format, negative amounts, and unexpected status values), and timeliness (latest_order and freshness_lag_hours) in a single partition-filtered scan. The second query measures consistency via a LEFT JOIN anti-join that counts order rows whose customer_id has no match in the customers dimension. Accuracy again is not here because it requires reconciliation to an external system.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
row_count=120357 | completeness_order_id_pct=100.0 | completeness_email_pct=98.1 | duplicate_order_ids=12 | pct_invalid_email=0.40 | pct_negative_amount=0.0 | pct_invalid_status=0.0 | latest_order=2026-07-02 04:00:00 | freshness_lag_hours=2

orphan_customer_ids=3
codeExamples.commonIssues: The email LIKE pattern is only a rough validity heuristic (use a regex function where available); ignoring timezone in DATEDIFF; running unpartitioned full scans on large fact tables.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Filter by partition/date to scale incrementally; use a regex function (e.g., REGEXP_LIKE) instead of LIKE for stricter validity; write the metric row into a dq_metrics history table so anomaly detection can flag drift versus static thresholds.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: An e-commerce company reports daily GMV (gross merchandise value) and new-customer counts to leadership and feeds an order-fulfillment model. Different upstream failures kept corrupting the numbers in different ways: a double-run load inflated GMV (uniqueness), null customer_ids broke joins (completeness), a delayed feed showed yesterday's data as today's (timeliness), and malformed currency codes crashed a downstream report (validity). The goal is to measure every quality dimension explicitly and block or quarantine bad data before it reaches consumers.
endToEndExample.inputData: A daily orders batch landing in a staging schema, where each order has order_id, customer_id, amount, currency, status, email, and order_date, plus a customers dimension table used for consistency checks.
endToEndExample.architecture: Ingestion writes raw orders to staging. A quality gate (dbt tests plus a Great Expectations suite) computes one metric per dimension, comparing each to a threshold and to a rolling baseline. Passing data loads to the trusted analytics layer; failing rows go to an orders_quarantine table with the failed-rule annotation. A dq_metrics history table feeds an anomaly-detection job and an observability dashboard, and alerts route to the owning team. Per-table SLAs are defined (fresh by 6 AM, zero duplicate order_ids, order_id completeness = 100%).
processingSteps: 1. Profiling computes per-column null counts, distinct counts, min/max amounts, currency value distribution, and the latest order_date, writing them to dq_metrics.
2. Completeness and uniqueness run: order_id must be 100% non-null and fully distinct; a duplicate_order_ids > 0 result flags the double-load case immediately.
3. Validity runs: currency must be in the ISO-4217 set, amount >= 0, status in the accepted set, and email must match the regex; violating rows are marked.
4. Timeliness and consistency run: freshness_lag_hours must be under the SLA, and every customer_id must exist in the customers dimension (referential integrity).

5. Row-level failures (invalid rows, duplicates) are routed to quarantine with the failed rule; aggregate/anomaly failures (row-count drop, null spike) block promotion; on any breach an alert fires with the failing dimension, measured value, threshold, and a link to the quarantined rows.
endToEndExample.output: A trusted orders table that is complete, valid, fresh, deduplicated, and referentially consistent; an orders_quarantine table holding rejected rows annotated by dimension; and a quality dashboard tracking each dimension's SLI (null rate, duplicate count, freshness lag, invalid-format rate) against its SLA over time.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Dashboards show, per dimension, the trend of completeness %, duplicate count, freshness lag hours, and invalid-format percentages, with baselines and anomaly detection flagging deviations like a sudden null spike or row-count drop.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Row-level dimension failures (validity, uniqueness) quarantine the offending rows and let the rest proceed; table-level and anomaly failures block promotion and alert; freshness (timeliness) breaches alert immediately. Quarantined rows are triaged and either fixed-and-reprocessed or confirmed as genuinely bad.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Leadership dashboards and the fulfillment model now consume only validated data. The double-load, null-key, stale-feed, and bad-currency incidents are each caught by their corresponding dimension check, mean-time-to-detection dropped from days to minutes, and consumers gained measurable, per-dimension confidence in the data.

industryUseCases.problem: Thousands of derived datasets had inconsistent, unclear quality, so analysts could not tell which tables to trust across dimensions like completeness and consistency.
industryUseCases.solution: Airbnb built dataset scoring and certification (the Midas/Dataportal effort) with standardized checks, ownership, and trust signals that surface quality to consumers.
industryUseCases.benefits: Consumers can quickly identify certified, high-quality datasets, reducing duplicated and untrustworthy tables and improving decision reliability across the company.

industryUseCases.problem: Teams discovered data-quality incidents (freshness lags, volume drops, schema changes, distribution shifts) only after stakeholders complained, causing 'data downtime'.
industryUseCases.solution: A data observability platform that continuously monitors freshness (timeliness), volume (completeness), schema, and distribution, learns baselines, and detects anomalies across the warehouse with lineage-aware root cause.
industryUseCases.benefits: Dimension breaches are detected automatically before consumers notice, cutting time-to-detection and time-to-resolution and reducing data downtime.

industryUseCases.problem: Validating quality dimensions like completeness, uniqueness, and validity on very large Spark datasets required efficient, declarative, automatable checks.
industryUseCases.solution: Amazon developed Deequ, a library for 'unit tests for data' that expresses completeness, uniqueness, and constraint (validity) checks and computes metrics with anomaly detection on Spark.
industryUseCases.benefits: Scalable, declarative per-dimension verification embedded in big-data pipelines, catching violations before bad data reaches downstream services and ML.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Compute all dimension metrics in one partition-filtered, set-based SQL pass pushed down to the warehouse or Spark; use approximate distinct counts (HyperLogLog) for uniqueness and sample rows for expensive validity/distribution checks so the checks scale with data growth.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Quarantine rows that fail row-level dimensions rather than dropping them, make dimension jobs idempotent so reruns are safe, and ensure a failure produces a clear recoverable state (failed batch with the offending dimension named) instead of a silent partial load.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Run the dimension gate as part of the orchestrated pipeline with retries and named ownership, and keep the dq_metrics history and quarantine tables on durable, replicated storage so quality state survives node failures.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Versioned dimension definitions and metric history let you reconstruct what 'good' looked like per dimension, and retained quarantined and source data enable safe reprocessing after recovery without losing failed records.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Combine completeness, uniqueness, validity, and timeliness metrics into a single scan; prefer set-based SQL over row-by-row Python; cache profiling baselines; and run expensive consistency joins and accuracy reconciliations less often than cheap freshness and null checks.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Tier dimensions by data value (all six on critical published tables, completeness plus freshness on intermediates), sample for expensive dimensions, and prune redundant or always-passing checks to cut compute spend.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Quarantine tables, profiling outputs, and failure logs may contain PII (invalid emails, mismatched records); apply masking, least-privilege access, and retention limits, and avoid emitting raw failing values into alerts.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track the five observability pillars (freshness, volume, schema, distribution, lineage) which map onto timeliness, completeness, validity, and consistency; expose each dimension as an SLI with baselines and anomaly detection and alert on breaches, not on every passing run.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Map every dimension to an explicit metric and check, validate at ingestion boundaries and before publication, reconcile counts/sums across source and target for accuracy, and store per-dimension results historically to enable trend analysis.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log each dimension's metric with batch and table context; route alerts to dataset owners with the failing dimension, measured value, threshold, and a link to quarantined rows; suppress noisy duplicate alerts and escalate only sustained or SLA-breaching failures.

recommendedPractices: **Map each of the six dimensions to a concrete metric and automated check** (completeness -> null rate, uniqueness -> duplicate count, validity -> regex/range, timeliness -> freshness lag, consistency -> referential join, accuracy -> reconciliation).
**Agree on explicit metric definitions** so 'completeness' or 'timeliness' means the same number to everyone.
**Handle accuracy separately** via reconciliation or sampled audits, since it cannot be self-checked from the data alone.
**Validate at boundaries**: run dimension checks on ingestion (untrusted input) and before publishing to consumers.
**Quarantine, don't drop**, rows that fail row-level dimensions so they can be inspected and reprocessed.
engineeringStandards: Dimension checks live in version control alongside pipeline/transformation code and run in both CI and production.
Every critical dataset has a named owner and a documented SLA expressed in dimension terms (freshness, completeness, uniqueness targets).
Failing dimension checks must gate promotion (block or quarantine) for critical data products, not merely warn.
designRecommendations: Tier dimensions by data value: all six on critical published tables, a lightweight subset (completeness, freshness) on transient intermediates.
Run cheap dimensions (completeness, timeliness) frequently and expensive ones (accuracy reconciliation, consistency joins) on a cadence.
Prefer engine pushdown and set-based SQL over row-by-row processing so dimension metrics scale.
namingConventions: Name checks by table + dimension + column, e.g., `orders__completeness__order_id_not_null` or `orders__uniqueness__order_id_unique`.
Name quarantine tables consistently, e.g., `orders_quarantine` or `<table>_dq_failures`.
documentationStandards: Document each table's target per dimension (freshness by 6 AM, order_id completeness 100%, zero duplicates) and its owner.
Document, for each check, which dimension it enforces, its metric, threshold, and severity (warn vs error).
Maintain a data catalog or Data Docs showing per-dimension trust/certification signals to consumers.
testingStrategies: Run dimension tests in CI against sample/staging data so logic or schema changes that break a dimension are caught pre-deploy.
Use fault injection (inject nulls, duplicates, stale timestamps, malformed values) to verify each dimension's check actually fails when it should.
Backtest anomaly thresholds for each dimension metric against historical incidents to tune sensitivity and reduce false positives.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing validity with accuracy and claiming the data is 'correct' because format checks pass.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Validity checks are easy to automate and give green results, so teams equate a passing regex with real-world correctness.
commonMistakes.impact: Well-formatted but wrong values (a valid-looking but incorrect phone number or amount) flow downstream and drive wrong decisions.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Treat validity and accuracy as separate dimensions; check validity with rules in the pipeline and verify accuracy by reconciling against a source of truth or sampled audits.

commonMistakes.mistake: Measuring only completeness (null checks) and calling it 'data quality'.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Null checks are the easiest dimension to compute, so teams stop there and ignore uniqueness, timeliness, consistency, and validity.
commonMistakes.impact: Duplicates inflate revenue, stale feeds show yesterday's numbers, and malformed values crash reports, all while the completeness dashboard is green.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Cover all six dimensions explicitly, each with its own metric and check, and track them together so no failure mode is invisible.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving dimension metrics undefined, so numbers are not comparable.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Different people define timeliness or completeness differently (records vs values, arrival time vs recency) without agreeing on a formula.
commonMistakes.impact: Teams argue about whether data is 'complete' or 'fresh', thresholds are inconsistent, and SLAs cannot be enforced.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Write down the exact metric for each dimension (e.g., completeness % = non_null / total, freshness lag = now - MAX(ts)) and version it with the pipeline.

comparisonSection.explanation: Validity confirms a value matches a defined rule (email regex, age 0-120) and is checkable from the data alone. Accuracy confirms the value is actually true and generally needs an external source of truth. A value can be valid but inaccurate (a well-formed but wrong email), which is why they are distinct dimensions.

Completeness measures missing data via null rate (COUNT(col) vs COUNT(*)) and answers 'is anything absent?'. Uniqueness measures unwanted repetition via COUNT(*) vs COUNT(DISTINCT key) and answers 'is anything doubled?'. A table can be 100% complete yet full of duplicates, or fully unique yet missing many values.

Timeliness asks whether the data is recent enough and arrived on schedule, measured as freshness lag against an SLA. Consistency asks whether the same fact agrees across records and systems, measured via reference joins and contradiction counts. Fresh data can still be inconsistent, and consistent data can still be stale.

beginnerQuestions.question: What are the six dimensions of data quality?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Completeness (no missing values or records), accuracy (matches real-world truth), consistency (no contradictions across systems), timeliness (fresh and on time), validity (conforms to formats, ranges, and rules), and uniqueness (no unwanted duplicates).
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Name all six and give a one-line example check per dimension (completeness -> null rate, uniqueness -> duplicate count); interviewers want to see you can operationalize each, not just recite them.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between validity and accuracy?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Validity means data conforms to a defined format or rule (an email matches the email regex, age is 0-120), and can be checked from the data alone. Accuracy means the value is actually correct in the real world (the email is the person's real email), and usually needs a source of truth. A value can be valid but inaccurate.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: The classic example is a well-formatted but wrong phone number: valid but not accurate. Stress that validity is automatable in-pipeline while accuracy needs reconciliation.

intermediateQuestions.question: How would you turn each data quality dimension into a concrete pipeline check?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Completeness -> null rate = COUNT(col)/COUNT(*); uniqueness -> duplicate count = COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT key); validity -> percentage matching a regex, accepted set, or range; timeliness -> freshness lag = now - MAX(timestamp) against an SLA; consistency -> referential/anti-join count of orphaned or contradictory rows; accuracy -> reconciliation match rate against a source of truth. Enforce them with dbt tests, Great Expectations, Soda, or Deequ, gating promotion or quarantining bad rows.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: A strong answer pairs every dimension with a specific metric and names the tools plus where the checks run (ingestion boundary, pre-publication).

intermediateQuestions.question: Which dimensions can be checked automatically in a pipeline, and which cannot?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, and uniqueness can be computed from the data itself plus reference tables, so they automate cleanly with dbt/Great Expectations/Soda/Deequ. Accuracy generally cannot be self-checked because you need an external source of truth; it is handled via reconciliation to another system, control totals, or sampled manual audits.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want you to recognize that accuracy is the odd one out and to describe the reconciliation/audit approach rather than pretending it is a simple in-pipeline test.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you measure accuracy at scale when you don't have a full source of truth?
advancedQuestions.answer: Use proxies and reconciliation: compare control totals or aggregates (row counts, sums) against an authoritative upstream system, join against reference/golden datasets for the fields you can verify, and run statistical sampling with manual audit to estimate an accuracy rate with a confidence interval. Track the sampled accuracy metric over time and alert on drops, and use anomaly detection on distributions to surface likely inaccuracies (sudden shifts) even without ground truth.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Emphasize reconciliation, sampling with confidence intervals, and distribution monitoring as accuracy proxies, and acknowledge you cannot achieve full accuracy verification without ground truth.

advancedQuestions.question: The completeness dashboard is green but revenue is wrong. Which dimensions would you investigate and how?
advancedQuestions.answer: Completeness being green rules out missing values, so I would check uniqueness first (duplicate_count = COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT key)) because doubled rows inflate revenue; then validity (negative or mis-scaled amounts, wrong currency codes); then consistency (orphaned customer_ids or amounts disagreeing with the billing system); then timeliness (a stale or partial feed showing an old snapshot). Each dimension has a distinct metric, so I isolate the failing one rather than guessing.
advancedQuestions.explanation: This tests whether you understand the dimensions are independent and can systematically eliminate them; the strongest signal is naming uniqueness first for inflated totals.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A daily report shows today's active-user count identical to yesterday's, but every value looks valid and nothing is null. Which dimension is likely failing and how do you confirm and prevent it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Values are valid and non-null, so completeness and validity look fine; identical-to-yesterday numbers point to a timeliness (freshness) failure where a stale snapshot was reloaded rather than fresh data. Confirm with a freshness metric and prevent with a freshness SLA check that gates publication.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Compute freshness_lag = now - MAX(event_timestamp); if the latest timestamp is a day old, the feed is stale and the pipeline republished yesterday's partition. Confirm the upstream load did not advance. Prevent recurrence by adding a timeliness check that fails the run when freshness_lag exceeds the SLA and when today's partition has no new max timestamp, plus a volume check so an unchanged row count alerts. Alert the owner with the freshness metric before the report publishes.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a dimension-based data quality layer for a company with hundreds of tables feeding analytics and ML, where consumers don't know which data to trust across dimensions.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: For each critical table, define an explicit metric per dimension (completeness null rate, uniqueness duplicate count, validity invalid-rate, timeliness freshness lag, consistency orphan count, accuracy reconciliation rate). Enforce the automatable five with pipeline-native tests (dbt/Great Expectations/Soda) at ingestion and pre-publication, handle accuracy via reconciliation jobs, quarantine failing rows, write all dimension metrics to a history store feeding anomaly detection, attach per-table SLAs and named owners, and surface per-dimension trust signals in a catalog. Observability monitors freshness/volume/schema/distribution across all tables.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Covering all six dimensions everywhere maximizes trust but adds maintenance, compute, and alert-fatigue risk, so tier rigor by data value. Static per-dimension thresholds are simple but brittle; anomaly detection on metric history adapts but needs tuning. Blocking on failure guarantees quality but can stall pipelines, so quarantine balances throughput and safety.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Compute dimension metrics with engine pushdown and set-based SQL, partition checks for incremental loads, use approximate distinct counts for uniqueness, run cheap dimensions (completeness, freshness) frequently and expensive ones (accuracy, consistency) on cadence, and centralize dimension definitions and alerting so the layer scales to hundreds of tables without bespoke per-table code.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: The dimensions of data quality (completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness) are the measurable attributes that judge fitness for use, each mapping to a concrete metric and automated pipeline check.
keyConcepts: Six dimensions: completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness.
Validity (conforms to a rule) vs accuracy (actually true): a value can be valid but inaccurate.
Five dimensions self-check in-pipeline; accuracy needs a source of truth.
Every dimension must become a single thresholdable metric.
Quarantine, don't drop, rows that fail row-level dimensions.
commands: SQL uniqueness: SELECT COUNT(*)-COUNT(DISTINCT key) FROM t;
SQL timeliness: SELECT DATEDIFF('hour', MAX(ts), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) FROM t;
dbt: not_null (completeness), unique (uniqueness), accepted_values/dbt_utils.accepted_range (validity), relationships (consistency); run `dbt test`
interviewPoints: Name and operationalize all six dimensions with a metric each.
Validity (format) vs accuracy (real-world truth) is the classic distinction.
Accuracy needs a source of truth; the other five are automatable.
Completeness (missing) vs uniqueness (duplicates) count opposite problems.
Turn each dimension into a thresholdable metric and quarantine failures.
quickNotes: Green completeness does not mean good data; check uniqueness, validity, timeliness too.
A valid value can still be inaccurate.
Define each dimension's exact metric so numbers are comparable.
Freshness lag = now - MAX(ts) is the go-to timeliness check.
Compute multiple dimension metrics in one set-based SQL scan for scale.

keyTakeaways: Data quality is judged across six dimensions (completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness), and each should map to one concrete, automatable metric.
Validity means a value follows a rule while accuracy means it is actually true; a value can be valid yet inaccurate, and accuracy is the one dimension that usually needs an external source of truth.

Completeness (null rate), uniqueness (duplicate count), validity (regex/range/accepted-set), timeliness (freshness lag), and consistency (referential joins) can all be checked automatically in a pipeline with dbt, Great Expectations, Soda, or Deequ.
Turn every dimension into a single thresholdable number, agree on its exact definition, validate at ingestion and before publication, and quarantine failing rows instead of dropping them.
Measuring only completeness is not data quality; cover all six dimensions together so failure modes like duplicates, staleness, and malformed values do not stay invisible behind a green null check.
